title: Cutting Involuntary Churn from Failed Payments for SaaS Businesses in Southeast Asia
summary: Failed recurring payments cause involuntary churn for SaaS businesses in SEA. See how Xendit recovers more renewals and protects recurring revenue.
body_markdown:
Recurring revenue looks predictable on a forecast, yet it only holds when every renewal actually collects. For


**SaaS businesses** across


**Southeast Asia** , the gap between the revenue you expect and the revenue you actually receive often comes down to


**involuntary churn** , meaning the subscribers you lose when a renewal payment fails and never recovers, even though they still wanted the service.


The scale of the opportunity explains why this deserves attention. The


[ASEAN cloud computing market](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/asean-cloud-computing-market) reached


**USD 21.78 billion in 2025** and is projected to grow to


**USD 48.74 billion by 2031** , with


**Software as a Service accounting for 55.65%** of that market in 2025.


As SaaS adoption widens across the region, more businesses are building revenue around


**monthly** ,


**annual** , and


**usage-based subscription models** , so a growing share of your income now depends on collections that repeat on a schedule.


Each billing cycle is another payment attempt that can fail. Reducing involuntary churn therefore comes down to how well your payment setup recovers a failed subscription renewal before it becomes a lost customer.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- How failed recurring payments create involuntary churn and put SaaS revenue at risk in Southeast Asia


- The specific reasons renewals fail, from expired cards to single-method dependence and weak recovery processes


- How Xendit recovers failed renewals with backup payment methods, automated retries, one-time Payment Links, and early notifications


- How usage-based billing keeps charges accurate for SaaS models priced on consumption or seats


- How accurate reporting and reconciliation keep finance operations manageable as subscription volume grows


The reasons recurring payments fail are specific and mostly within your control, so understanding them is the first step toward keeping more of your recurring revenue.


## **Why failed recurring payments put SaaS revenue at risk**


SaaS businesses do not all collect revenue the same way. Alongside subscriptions, many also charge for one-time purchases, add-ons, and pay-as-you-go usage, and any of these payments can fail at the point of collection.


**Involuntary churn** , though, comes specifically from


**failed recurring charges** , because a subscription only holds when every renewal clears over time.


As your subscriber base grows, a single payment issue affects a larger share of predictable revenue than it did when you had fewer customers. A failed renewal rarely means someone wants to cancel, but without a reliable way to recover it, the subscription still ends and the revenue still stops.


Recurring payments in SaaS fail in several distinct ways, and each one drives involuntary churn unless your business can recover it:


### **1. A successful sign-up does not guarantee renewal**


Converting a customer happens once, while collecting payment from them happens on every billing cycle. Payment details can expire, an account can have insufficient funds on the billing date, or a technical issue can interrupt a later cycle while the customer still intends to keep using your product.


For your business, the initial sign-up secures only the first payment, and each renewal after it can still fail to collect.


### **2. Depending on one payment method removes your fallback**


When a subscription runs on only one payment method, usually a credit or debit card, a declined charge leaves no other route to complete the charge. This carries more weight in Southeast Asia, where many customers hold funds in e-wallets or bank accounts and use cards infrequently, so a card-only setup limits who can subscribe and leaves customers no alternative when their main payment method fails.


Without a second payment option to fall back on, a charge that could have gone through on another method turns into a lost renewal instead.


### **3. A declined payment becomes a cancellation without a recovery path**


One declined charge does not have to end a subscription, though it will if nothing follows the decline. With no backup methods and no structured retry process, a temporary failure leads to suspended access and eventual cancellation. Whether a failed payment becomes a brief interruption or a permanent loss usually depends on the recovery process behind it.


### **4. Customers often do not know a renewal has failed**


Many subscribers only notice a failed renewal when their access to the service stops, and by then the experience may have already soured. If nothing prompts them at the moment the charge declines, they lose the chance to fix something as simple as a low balance or an updated card.


For your business, prompting the customer as soon as the charge fails, for example with a notice about the missed payment, recovers renewals that would otherwise lapse because the customer never knew the payment had failed.


### **5. Manual recovery gets harder as subscriptions scale**


At low volume, a finance or customer-success team can chase failed payments by hand, spotting each failure, contacting the customer, resending instructions, and confirming the result. That workload climbs in step with your subscriber count, so a process that works at a few hundred subscribers becomes unmanageable at several thousand. Recovery built on manual effort quietly caps how far your subscription base can grow before operations break down.


### **6. Fixed billing does not fit every SaaS model**


Flat monthly or annual billing suits standard plans, but many SaaS businesses charge on usage, seats, or consumption that changes each cycle. A setup locked to one amount cannot bill variable charges accurately, which forces workarounds that create their own errors and failures. Matching the billing model to how you actually price your product keeps charges correct and cuts the disputes and declines that come from billing the wrong amount.

## **How Xendit reduces involuntary churn for SaaS businesses**


[Xendit Subscriptions](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/subscriptions/) lets your business schedule recurring collections on daily, weekly, monthly, or annual cycles, while you set the payment amount, billing dates, retry rules, and customer notifications for each plan. Customers link a payment method once, and eligible future charges then process automatically without asking them to enter details again.


What matters most for involuntary churn is how the system responds when one of those automatic charges fails. Xendit works against that churn on two fronts, through


**single payment options** that recover an individual failed charge and through


**subscription**[features](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/subscriptions-features) that automate collection and recovery across the whole billing relationship:


### **1. Reduce churn with single payment options**


When a scheduled charge fails, the quickest way to save a subscription is often a


**single payment the customer completes right away** , and some SaaS revenue does not run on a schedule at all:


- **One-time**[Payment Links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/payment-links/) **for recovery** When an automatic charge fails, Xendit can send the customer a[one-time Payment Link](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payment-1) to settle that specific cycle using any payment method, including one not attached to the subscription. Xendit sends the notification carrying the Payment Link automatically for each failed attempt, and once the customer pays, that cycle is settled and no further attempts are made for it. The method used for the Payment Link is not stored, so later cycles continue on the originally attached methods. This hands control to the customer and recovers the renewal through a single payment before you write it off as churned.


- **Saved methods for one-time and add-on charges** Not all SaaS revenue is recurring, since many businesses also bill for one-time purchases, add-ons, and pay-as-you-go usage. Xendit lets you securely store a customer's card as an[unscheduled card on file](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-integrations) and charge these single payments when you need to, without a fixed billing schedule. Collecting these one-off charges reliably protects the revenue you earn outside your subscription plans.


### **2. Reduce churn with subscription payments**


For the recurring side of your revenue, Xendit


**automates collection** so every renewal has several chances to clear before it lapses:


- **Multiple payment methods with a set priority order** You can attach up to five payment channels to a single subscriber's plan and set the order Xendit should charge them in. For each payment attempt, Xendit works through the attached channels in the priority you set, so a failed charge on the first channel moves the payment automatically to the second, and onward through the list before the retry status is summarized. This gives every renewal several routes to succeed instead of one, which directly answers the payment failure that would otherwise end the subscription.


- **Automated retries timed around customer funding** A failed charge is often a matter of timing, since a customer may top up an e-wallet or restore a bank balance a day or two after a charge fails. Xendit manages[retries](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/recover-failed-payments) automatically using the configuration you set when creating the plan, reattempting the charge across the attached channels with no action from your team. Your systems receive webhooks, the automated status messages that report each cycle as successful, failed, or still in retries, so your records stay current in real time. Automated retries recover a meaningful share of failures that clear on a second or third attempt, and they do it without adding manual work for your team.


- **Notifications that surface a failure early** Xendit sends automated email or WhatsApp notifications for subscription confirmations, missed payments, and completed charges, so customers hear about a failed renewal when it happens instead of when their access stops. That prompt often recovers a renewal through one simple customer action, which closes the communication gap that lets willing subscribers slip away.


- **Card handling without PCI certification** For customers who do pay by card, Xendit collects and[tokenizes their card](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/create-a-token) details through a Xendit-hosted page, storing the card as a secure token so your business can process recurring card charges without holding PCI-DSS certification, the security standard that governs how card data is handled. This keeps card-based renewals secure and compliant while taking the certification burden off your own engineering roadmap.


- **Usage-based billing for variable pricing** Many SaaS businesses charge on consumption instead of a flat fee, and Xendit supports[usage-based subscriptions](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/usage-based-subscriptions) where the amount collected changes each cycle based on what the customer used before a cut-off point. You set the charge for each upcoming cycle through the Update Cycle API before the scheduled billing date, and Xendit notifies you of every new cycle so the correct amount is in place in time. For metered or seat-based pricing, this keeps each charge accurate, which prevents the disputes and failed payments that come from billing a fixed amount when real usage differs.


- **Local payment coverage across the region** Recovering renewals across Southeast Asia also depends on offering methods customers keep funded, which differs from one market to the next. Xendit provides access to[more than 100 payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) across Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Singapore, and Hong Kong through a single API and dashboard, so you can add locally relevant options as primary or backup methods without building a separate integration for each country. A customer paying through a method they use daily is less likely to fail a future charge, which strengthens both sign-up conversion and renewal reliability.

[Mekari](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/mekari/) , a SaaS company that combines invoicing, payment, and accounting on one platform, used

**140% payment-volume growth** from 2021 to 2022 and made its monthly


**reconciliation 5x faster** .


The lesson for your business is that the same payment infrastructure that recovers renewals can also keep reconciliation manageable as volume grows, so finance operations do not turn into the bottleneck that scaling subscriptions tends to create.

## **FAQ for SaaS businesses in Southeast Asia: Reducing involuntary churn from failed payments**


### **What causes involuntary churn in a SaaS subscription business?**


Involuntary churn happens when a subscription ends because a renewal payment failed, even though the customer still wanted to keep the service. The usual triggers are expired cards, insufficient funds on the billing date, technical interruptions, and payment methods that customers rarely keep topped up.


**Xendit** reduces these losses with automated retries, backup payment methods, and


[recovery links](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/recover-failed-payments) that give each failed renewal several chances to clear before it becomes a cancellation.


### **How can a SaaS business recover failed recurring payments automatically?**


Automatic recovery pairs retry logic with backup payment methods so a declined charge is reattempted without anyone stepping in.


**Xendit** runs retries according to the rules you set when


[creating a subscription plan](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-subscriptions-work) , working through the attached payment channels and reporting each attempt through webhooks. If the retries do not succeed, Xendit can send the customer a


[one-time Payment Link](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payment-1) to settle that cycle, giving the renewal a final route to recover.


### **Can you add a backup payment method to a subscription plan?**


Yes. A subscription that runs on one method has no backup when that method declines, which is a common source of lost renewals.


**Xendit** lets you attach up to five payment channels to a single plan and


[set their priority order](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/subscriptions-features) , so a failed charge on the primary channel moves automatically to the next one before the subscription is treated as churned.


### **Can Xendit handle usage-based billing for SaaS pricing?**


Yes. Plenty of SaaS businesses charge on consumption or seats that change each cycle, which a fixed billing amount cannot capture accurately.


**Xendit** supports


[usage-based subscriptions](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/usage-based-subscriptions) where you set the amount for each upcoming cycle through the Update Cycle API before the billing date, so customers are charged for what they actually used and billing errors that lead to failed or disputed charges are reduced.


### **How do you collect recurring SaaS payments where customers do not use cards?**


Across much of Southeast Asia, customers keep money in e-wallets and bank accounts and use cards infrequently, so card-only billing limits both sign-ups and renewals.


**Xendit** gives your business access to


[more than 100 payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) across its operating markets in the region through one integration, so you can collect recurring payments through the local methods customers already use and keep renewals clearing on methods they keep funded.
